records.source: מַשָּׂ֖א נִֽינְוֵ֑ה סֵ֧פֶר חֲז֛וֹן נַח֖וּם הָאֶלְקֹשִֽׁי׃
records.gloss: The oracle of Nineveh. [The] book of [the] vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.
pieces: An oracle about Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum of Elkosh.

L.1: The oracle [concerning] Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.

R.1: This is a message about Nineveh. It is the book of the vision that Nahum from Elkosh received.

decisions.choice: oracle: a solemn pronouncement from God, here a word of judgment on a city
decisions.reason: The noun comes from the verb "lift up": a word lifted up, that is, pronounced. It heads many of the prophets' words against the nations (Isaiah 13:1; 15:1; 17:1), and Habakkuk 1:1 opens the same way. It can also mean a load that is carried, a "burden", but here it names the kind of message that follows (see Isaiah 13:1).

decisions.choice: Nineveh: the capital of the Assyrian empire, destroyed in 612 BC
decisions.reason: Nineveh stood on the east bank of the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul in Iraq. Under Sennacherib (about 705-681 BC) it became the capital of Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and made Judah pay tribute (2 Kings 17-19). In 612 BC an alliance of Babylonians and Medes besieged the city and destroyed it, and the empire collapsed a few years later. Nahum's three chapters announce that fall. They were spoken after the fall of Thebes in Egypt (3:8-10, about 663 BC) and before 612 BC. A century or so earlier, in the book of Jonah, the same city had repented and been spared (Jonah 3:10).

decisions.choice: Nahum the Elkoshite: Nahum from the town of Elkosh, whose site is unknown
decisions.reason: The name Nahum means "comfort" or "comforter", a fitting name for a prophet whose message is comfort for Judah (1:12-13; 2:1). "Elkoshite" names his home town. Several places have been suggested, in Galilee, in Judah and near Nineveh, but none can be shown to be right. Nothing else is known about him.

decisions.choice: the book of the vision: a written record of what the prophet saw
decisions.reason: "Vision" is the usual word for a prophet's message from God, as in Isaiah 1:1 and Obadiah 1, whether it came by sight or by word. This is the only heading among the prophets that calls the message a "book", a written scroll, which may mean that it was written down from the start.

decisions.choice: An oracle (B); a message (R); of Elkosh (B); from Elkosh (R)
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah 13:1, Literal and Balanced say "oracle" and Readable says "message". Balanced and Readable say "of" or "from Elkosh" for "the Elkoshite", and Readable says that Nahum received the vision.

records.heading: The jealous and avenging God

records.source: אֵ֣ל קַנּ֤וֹא וְנֹקֵם֙ יְהוָ֔ה נֹקֵ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה וּבַ֣עַל חֵמָ֑ה נֹקֵ֤ם יְהוָה֙ לְצָרָ֔יו וְנוֹטֵ֥ר ה֖וּא לְאֹיְבָֽיו׃
records.gloss: A God jealous and avenging [is] Yahweh; avenging [is] Yahweh and a lord of wrath; avenging [is] Yahweh on his adversaries, and keeping [wrath is] he for his enemies.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is a jealous and avenging God; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} avenges and is full of wrath. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} takes vengeance on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} foes \q and holds {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger against {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies.

L.2: A jealous and avenging God [is] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [is] avenging and a master of wrath; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} takes vengeance on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} adversaries, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} keeps [wrath] for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies.

R.2: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is a jealous God who punishes wrongdoing. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} punishes, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger is fierce. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} punishes those who oppose {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. \q He stays angry with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies.

decisions.choice: verses 2-8 are a partial alphabet poem, from aleph to kaph
alternatives: no acrostic was intended, and the letters fall in order by chance
decisions.reason: Lines in these verses begin, more or less in order, with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet: aleph in verse 2, beth in the second half of verse 3, gimel in verse 4, then he and waw in verse 5, zayin and heth in verse 6, teth and yod in verse 7, and kaph in verse 8. The pattern is not complete: the letter for daleth in verse 4 is missing (see the note there), some letters stand at the second word of a line rather than the first, and after kaph the order breaks off. Some readers trace it further into verses 9-14, but only by changing the text. How far the poem was meant as an acrostic, and whether it once ran through the whole alphabet, cannot be known. Like the acrostics of Lamentations, it gives the poem a sense of order and completeness: the LORD's judgment is full and orderly, from first to last.

decisions.choice: jealous: zealous for the loyalty that belongs to him alone
decisions.reason: This form of the word is used only here and in Joshua 24:19. A related form is in the commandments: "I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). It is the passion of one who will not share what belongs to him: the loyalty of his people, and his own honor. It also turns to protect his people against those who attack them (Zechariah 1:14-15; Joel 2:18). It is not petty envy.

decisions.choice: avenging: punishing wrongs as a ruler and judge does
decisions.reason: The verb, used three times in a row, is the act of a king or judge who sees that a wrong is punished and the wronged are set right. Scripture forbids people to take revenge for themselves and leaves vengeance to God (Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19). Here the wrong is Assyria's cruelty to the nations and to Judah (3:1, 19).

decisions.choice: a master of wrath ... keeps wrath: his anger is real and does not simply lapse
decisions.reason: "Master of wrath" is a Hebrew way of saying that someone is full of wrath, as "master of dreams" (Genesis 37:19) means a dreamer. "Keep" with no object is used of keeping anger (Leviticus 19:18; Psalm 103:9; Jeremiah 3:5): he holds it against his enemies. The next verse balances this: he is slow to anger.

decisions.choice: a master of wrath (L); full of wrath (B); his anger is fierce (R); keeps [wrath] (L); holds his anger (B); stays angry (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew picture and brackets the word "wrath", which the verb implies. Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (m4). Readable says "punishes" for "avenges", because "revenge" in English suggests personal spite (m3), and adds "wrongdoing" to make the object plain.

records.source: יְהֹוָ֗ה אֶ֤רֶךְ אַפַּ֨יִם֙ וּגְדָל־כֹּ֔חַ וְנַקֵּ֖ה לֹ֣א יְנַקֶּ֑ה יְהוָ֗ה בְּסוּפָ֤ה וּבִשְׂעָרָה֙ דַּרְכּ֔וֹ וְעָנָ֖ן אֲבַ֥ק רַגְלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: Yahweh [is] long of anger and great of power, and to leave unpunished not he will leave unpunished. Yahweh, in storm-wind and in storm [is] his way, and clouds [are the] dust of his feet.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is slow to grow angry but great in power, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will never acquit the guilty. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} makes {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} way in the whirlwind and the storm, \q and the clouds are the dust of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.

L.3: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} [is] long of anger and great in power, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will by no means acquit [the guilty]. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, in whirlwind and in storm [is] {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} way, \q and clouds [are] the dust of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.

R.3: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is slow to become angry, but {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power is great. \q He will not let the guilty go free. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} travels in the whirlwind and the storm. \q The clouds are like dust kicked up by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet.

decisions.choice: slow to anger ... will by no means acquit: the words of Exodus 34:6-7, with "great in power" in place of "great in loyal love"
decisions.reason: When the LORD proclaimed his name to Moses he said that he is "slow to anger and great in loyal love and faithfulness", forgiving sin, "but he will by no means acquit the guilty" (Exodus 34:6-7). Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2 quote the merciful side of these words. Nahum quotes the start and the end, and where Exodus says "great in loyal love" he says "great in power". The point is not that God has stopped being merciful (verse 7 says he is good to those who trust him), but that his patience is not weakness. Jonah complained that God's mercy spared Nineveh (Jonah 4:2); Nahum announces that the same God will not leave the city's guilt unpunished for ever.

decisions.choice: will by no means acquit: the verb repeated for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "and leaving unpunished, he will not leave unpunished", a verb doubled to make it certain, the same phrase as Exodus 34:7. The object, "the guilty", is not stated but is plain from Exodus.

decisions.choice: whirlwind, storm and clouds: the LORD comes as in a great storm
decisions.reason: Scripture often pictures the LORD's coming to judge or rescue as a storm, with wind, cloud, thunder and an earthquake (Exodus 19:16-18; Psalm 18:8-16; Habakkuk 3). Clouds are his chariot (Psalm 104:3); here they are the dust his feet kick up, so great is he.

decisions.choice: long of anger (L), slow to grow angry (B), slow to become angry (R); will by no means acquit (L), will never acquit (B), will not let the guilty go free (R)
decisions.reason: These are the words of Exodus 34:6-7 as already published, kept at each level so that the reader hears the echo (m1). Where Exodus has *hesed* Nahum has "power", so the open question of how to word *hesed* in these quotations does not touch this verse. The prophets use "loyal love" (Literal, Balanced) and "faithful love" (Readable), pending the founder's ruling; the published Exodus 34:6 has "steadfast love" at Literal. Literal brackets "the guilty", which the Hebrew leaves unstated.

decisions.choice: like dust kicked up by his feet
decisions.reason: Readable adds "like" and "kicked up" so that the picture is not read as a statement that clouds are dust.

records.source: גּוֹעֵ֤ר בַּיָּם֙ וַֽיַּבְּשֵׁ֔הוּ וְכָל־הַנְּהָר֖וֹת הֶֽחֱרִ֑יב אֻמְלַ֤ל בָּשָׁן֙ וְכַרְמֶ֔ל וּפֶ֥רַח לְבָנ֖וֹן אֻמְלָֽל׃
records.gloss: Rebuking the sea and he dried it up, and all the rivers he has dried up; withered [are] Bashan and Carmel, and [the] blossom of Lebanon has withered.
pieces: He rebukes the sea and makes it dry; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} dries up every river. \q Bashan and Carmel wilt, \q and the flowers of Lebanon fade.

L.4: He rebukes the sea and makes it dry, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} dries up all the rivers; \q Bashan and Carmel wither, \q and the bloom of Lebanon withers.

R.4: He gives an order to the sea, and it dries up. \q He makes all the rivers run dry. \q The rich pastures of Bashan and Carmel dry up, \q and the flowers of Lebanon wither.

decisions.choice: rebuking the sea and drying the rivers: the LORD's power over the waters
decisions.reason: The LORD "rebuked the Red Sea and it dried up" when Israel left Egypt (Psalm 106:9), and the Jordan stopped flowing before them (Joshua 3:16). The same words are used of his power over the sea and the floods in Isaiah 50:2 and Psalm 104:7. In the poetry of the ancient world the sea stood for the forces of chaos; the LORD commands it with a word.

decisions.choice: Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon: the most fertile places in the land
decisions.reason: Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its cattle and oaks (Amos 4:1; Isaiah 2:13); Carmel, the ridge by the sea, for its gardens and woods; Lebanon for its cedars and flowers. If even these wither when the LORD comes, nothing can stand before him. Isaiah 33:9 names the same places.

decisions.choice: withers ... withers: the same verb twice
alternatives: a different verb meaning "languish", beginning with daleth
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has the same verb at the start and the end of the second line. In the alphabet pattern of verses 2-8 (see verse 2), the first of them stands where a word beginning with daleth is expected. A verb of the same sense that begins with that letter has therefore been suggested in its place. No change in the sense follows, and the translation keeps the text as it stands.

decisions.choice: gives an order to (R); the rich pastures of (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "gives an order" for "rebukes", since the sea obeys a command, and adds "the rich pastures of" so that the reader knows why Bashan and Carmel are named (m2).

records.source: הָרִים֙ רָעֲשׁ֣וּ מִמֶּ֔נּוּ וְהַגְּבָע֖וֹת הִתְמֹגָ֑גוּ וַתִּשָּׂ֤א הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ מִפָּנָ֔יו וְתֵבֵ֖ל וְכָל־יֹ֥שְׁבֵי בָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: [The] mountains quake because of him, and the hills melt; and the earth heaves up from before him, and [the] world and all [who] dwell in it.
pieces: Before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} the mountains quake, \q and the hills melt away. \q The earth heaves at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} presence, \q the world and everyone who lives in it.

L.5: [The] mountains quake because of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, \q and the hills melt; \q the earth heaves before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, \q the world and all who dwell in it.

R.5: The mountains shake when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes, \q and the hills melt away. \q The earth trembles when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} appears, \q the whole world and everyone who lives in it.

decisions.choice: mountains quake and hills melt: the earth's response to God's coming
decisions.reason: The same picture is in Judges 5:5, Psalm 97:5 and Micah 1:4. It does not describe one particular earthquake but the trembling of the whole creation before its maker when he comes to judge.

decisions.choice: the earth heaves: it rises and shakes as in an earthquake
alternatives: the earth is laid waste before him
decisions.reason: The verb means "lift up". Used of the earth, it pictures the ground heaving. Some take it as "the earth is laid waste" by reading a verb of similar sound, but the plain sense of the word fits the quaking mountains.

decisions.choice: when he comes; when he appears
decisions.reason: Readable says "when he comes" and "when he appears" for "before him", since the verses describe the LORD's coming (verse 3).

records.source: לִפְנֵ֤י זַעְמוֹ֙ מִ֣י יַֽעֲמ֔וֹד וּמִ֥י יָק֖וּם בַּחֲר֣וֹן אַפּ֑וֹ חֲמָתוֹ֙ נִתְּכָ֣ה כָאֵ֔שׁ וְהַצֻּרִ֖ים נִתְּצ֥וּ מִמֶּֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: Before his indignation who can stand? And who can rise up in [the] burning of his anger? His wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are torn down by him.
pieces: Who can stand before {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} indignation? \q Who can endure {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} burning anger? \q His wrath pours out like fire, \q and the rocks are shattered before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.6: Before {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} indignation, who can stand? \q And who can endure the burning of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger? \q His fury is poured out as fire, \q and the rocks are torn apart by {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.6: Who can stand up to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fury? \q Who can survive when {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger burns? \q His anger pours out like fire. \q He breaks the rocks to pieces.

decisions.choice: who can stand ... who can endure: questions that expect the answer "no one"
decisions.reason: The questions are not asking for information. They declare that no one can withstand the LORD's anger, as in Joel 2:11, Malachi 3:2 and Psalm 76:8.

decisions.choice: poured out like fire ... the rocks are broken down
decisions.reason: Wrath poured out like fire suggests molten metal or lava flowing (compare Jeremiah 7:20). The second verb means to pull down or break apart, used of walls and altars (Judges 6:30-32); even rock, the most solid thing in nature, gives way.

decisions.choice: stand up to; survive when his anger burns
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the questions but uses everyday words: "stand up to" for standing before an opponent, and "survive" for "endure" or "rise up".

records.source: ט֣וֹב יְהוָ֔ה לְמָע֖וֹז בְּי֣וֹם צָרָ֑ה וְיֹדֵ֖עַ חֹ֥סֵי בֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Good [is] Yahweh, for a refuge in a day of trouble; and [he is] knowing those [who] take refuge in him.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is good, \q a stronghold in the day of trouble; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} knows those who take refuge in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.7: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} [is] good, \q a stronghold in [the] day of distress, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} knows those who take refuge in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.7: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is good. \q He is a safe place when trouble comes. \q He cares for those who run to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for safety.

decisions.choice: the LORD is good: the other side of the same power
decisions.reason: Between the storm of verses 2-6 and the flood of verse 8 the poem says that the LORD is good. The power that crushes his enemies is the shelter of those who trust him. The whole book holds these together: judgment on Nineveh is comfort for Judah.

decisions.choice: a stronghold in the day of trouble
decisions.reason: The word is a fortress or place of safety, used of God in Psalm 27:1; 31:3 and 37:39. "The day of trouble" is any time of distress (Psalm 50:15), here Assyria's oppression.

decisions.choice: knows: cares for and acknowledges as his own
decisions.reason: To "know" people often means to care for them and take them as one's own: "the LORD knows the way of the righteous" (Psalm 1:6; Amos 3:2). Those who "take refuge" in him are those who trust him, as in Psalm 2:12.

decisions.choice: a safe place; cares for; run to him for safety
decisions.reason: Readable says "safe place" for "stronghold", "cares for" for "knows" (m3) and "run to him for safety" for "take refuge in him".

records.source: וּבְשֶׁ֣טֶף עֹבֵ֔ר כָּלָ֖ה יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה מְקוֹמָ֑הּ וְאֹיְבָ֖יו יְרַדֶּף־חֹֽשֶׁךְ׃
records.gloss: And with a flood passing over, a complete end he will make of her place, and his enemies he will pursue [into] darkness.
pieces: But with a rushing flood \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will make an end of her place, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will drive {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies into darkness.

L.8: But with a flood passing over \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will make a full end of her place, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will pursue {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies [into] darkness.

R.8: But like a flood that sweeps everything away, \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will completely destroy the place where Nineveh stands. \q He will chase {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} enemies into darkness.

decisions.choice: her place: the site of the city, Nineveh
alternatives: those who rise up against him (Greek)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "her place". Nineveh, named in 1:1, is the "her" of the book (2:2, 8-9; 3:7), so this means the city and its site: the flood will leave no place where it stood. The Greek translation, with different vowels, reads "those who rise up against him", which matches "his enemies" in the next line. The translation follows the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: an overflowing flood: an overwhelming judgment
decisions.reason: A flood that sweeps over the land is a common picture of an invading army (Isaiah 8:7-8; Daniel 9:26). Nahum may also have in mind the waters that played a part in the fall of Nineveh (2:7, 9).

decisions.choice: he will pursue his enemies into darkness
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets "darkness" after the verb with no preposition. It may mean that the LORD drives his enemies into darkness, or that darkness pursues them. Darkness here is death and ruin, the opposite of light and life.

decisions.choice: the place where Nineveh stands
decisions.reason: Readable names Nineveh, because "her place" has no clear reference in this verse without it (m1).

records.source: מַה־תְּחַשְּׁבוּן֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה כָּלָ֖ה ה֣וּא עֹשֶׂ֑ה לֹֽא־תָק֥וּם פַּעֲמַ֖יִם צָרָֽה׃
records.gloss: What do you plot against Yahweh? A complete end he [is] making; not will rise up twice trouble.
pieces: What are you plotting against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? \q He will make a complete end; \q trouble will not rise up a second time.

L.9: What do you plot against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? \q He is making a full end; \q trouble will not rise up twice.

R.9: What are you planning against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? \q He will put a complete end to it. \q Trouble will not come a second time.

decisions.choice: What do you plot: a challenge to those who plan against the LORD
alternatives: Whatever you plot against the LORD, he will make an end of it
decisions.reason: The question may also be read as "Whatever you plot against the LORD, he will make an end of it". "You" is plural. It is most likely addressed to the Assyrians, whose plans against Judah were plans against the LORD (verse 11). Some take it as addressed to doubters in Judah, who thought the LORD could not deal with Assyria.

decisions.choice: trouble will not rise up twice: one blow will be enough
alternatives: the distress Assyria brought will not come again
decisions.reason: The line may mean that the LORD's blow on Assyria will be so complete that it will not need to be struck again (compare 1 Samuel 26:8), or that the distress Assyria brought on Judah will not come again (verse 12). Both point to a final end.

decisions.choice: planning; put a complete end to it
decisions.reason: Readable says "planning" for "plotting" and adds "to it", meaning the plotting.

records.source: כִּ֚י עַד־סִירִ֣ים סְבֻכִ֔ים וּכְסָבְאָ֖ם סְבוּאִ֑ים אֻ֨כְּל֔וּ כְּקַ֥שׁ יָבֵ֖שׁ מָלֵֽא׃
records.gloss: For [though] like thorns entangled, and like their drink drunken, they will be consumed like stubble dry fully.
pieces: Though they are like a tangle of thorns \q and drunk with their wine, \q they will be burned up \q like dry stubble.

L.10: For though [they are] like entangled thorns, \q and drunk as with their drink, \q they will be consumed \q like stubble fully dry.

R.10: They are like a tangle of thorn bushes, \q like drunkards soaked in wine. \q But they will be burned up \q like dry straw.

decisions.choice: a very difficult verse: entangled thorns, drunkards, dry stubble
alternatives: until they are like entangled thorns
decisions.reason: Almost every phrase of this verse is hard. The first words may mean "though they are like thorns" or "until they are like thorns"; "drunk with their drink" is a play on similar-sounding words; and the last word, "fully", may belong with the next verse. The general sense is clear: however strong and tangled the enemy is, and however much they drink, they will be burned up as quickly as dry straw.

decisions.choice: thorns and stubble burn quickly
decisions.reason: Thorn bushes and stubble catch fire at once and burn out fast (Isaiah 10:17; Psalm 118:12; Malachi 3:19). Drunkenness returns in 3:11, where Nineveh is told she will be made drunk with the cup of judgment.

decisions.choice: drunkards soaked in wine; dry straw
decisions.reason: Readable says "soaked in wine" for "drunk with their drink" and "straw" for "stubble".

records.source: מִמֵּ֣ךְ יָצָ֔א חֹשֵׁ֥ב עַל־יְהוָ֖ה רָעָ֑ה יֹעֵ֖ץ בְּלִיָּֽעַל׃ס
records.gloss: From you has come out [one who] plots against Yahweh evil, a counselor of worthlessness.
pieces: From you has come one \q who plots evil against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q a counselor of wickedness.

L.11: From you has come out \q one who plots evil against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q a counselor of worthlessness.

R.11: Nineveh, from you came a man \q who made evil plans against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q His advice was wicked and worthless.

decisions.choice: from you: from Nineveh
decisions.reason: "You" is feminine singular. After the plural of verse 9 the poem turns to a city, which is Nineveh (1:1; 2:2).

decisions.choice: one who plots evil against the LORD: an Assyrian king
decisions.reason: The text does not name him. The words fit an Assyrian king who planned against Jerusalem, such as Sennacherib, who besieged it in 701 BC and mocked the LORD (2 Kings 18:13-35; Isaiah 36-37). The same pattern of plotting and defeat is then applied to Nineveh's rulers as a whole.

decisions.choice: worthlessness: the wickedness of one who is good for nothing
decisions.reason: The word joins "without" and "use" or "profit". It describes people who are worthless and wicked (Deuteronomy 13:14; 1 Samuel 2:12). In later Jewish writing it became a name for the devil, Belial (2 Corinthians 6:15); here it describes the Assyrian. It returns in 2:1.

decisions.choice: a counselor of wickedness (B); his advice was wicked and worthless (R); Nineveh (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "wickedness" for the Hebrew word, which carries both senses (m3); Readable keeps both. Readable names Nineveh, the "you" of the verse (m1).

records.source: כֹּ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אִם־שְׁלֵמִים֙ וְכֵ֣ן רַבִּ֔ים וְכֵ֥ן נָגֹ֖זּוּ וְעָבָ֑ר וְעִ֨נִּתִ֔ךְ לֹ֥א אֲעַנֵּ֖ךְ עֽוֹד׃
records.gloss: Thus says Yahweh: Though [they are] whole and likewise many, even so they will be cut off, and he will pass away; and I have afflicted you, I will not afflict you again.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: Though they are at full strength and many, \q they will still be cut down and pass away. \q I have afflicted you, \q but I will afflict you no more.

L.12: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Though [they are] at full strength and likewise many, \q even so they will be sheared off, and he will pass away. \q I have afflicted you; \q I will not afflict you again.

R.12: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: Even though the Assyrians are strong and have many soldiers, \q they will be cut down and disappear. \q People of Judah, I have made you suffer, \q but I will not make you suffer again.

decisions.choice: they ... you: the LORD speaks of the Assyrians and to Judah
decisions.reason: "They" are the Assyrians. "You" is feminine singular and is Judah, pictured as a woman, as 2:1 makes plain. The poem keeps turning from one to the other: verse 11 speaks to Nineveh, verses 12-13 to Judah, verse 14 to the Assyrian king, and 2:1 to Judah again. The verb "pass away" is singular, perhaps thinking of the army as one body or of its king.

decisions.choice: at full strength: whole, unharmed and complete in number
decisions.reason: The word means whole or complete. It may describe the Assyrians as at full strength, or as having allies; the parallel "many" favors their numbers and strength. The point is that being strong will not save them.

decisions.choice: I have afflicted you: Assyria was the LORD's rod for Judah
decisions.reason: The prophets say that the LORD used Assyria to discipline his people (Isaiah 10:5-6). That discipline is now over. Nahum does not say that Judah was never at fault, but that the LORD's punishment through Assyria has come to an end.

decisions.choice: Thus says the LORD (L); The LORD says this (B); This is what the LORD says (R)
decisions.reason: The settled wording of the formula in the prophets (Isaiah). God's words follow without quotation marks.

decisions.choice: the Assyrians ... have many soldiers; People of Judah
decisions.reason: Readable names the two groups the verse speaks of and to (m1), since the Hebrew does it only by "they" and "you".

records.heading: No more affliction for Judah

records.source: וְעַתָּ֕ה אֶשְׁבֹּ֥ר מֹטֵ֖הוּ מֵֽעָלָ֑יִךְ וּמוֹסְרֹתַ֖יִךְ אֲנַתֵּֽק׃
records.gloss: And now I will break his yoke-bar from on you, and your bonds I will tear apart.
pieces: Now I will break his yoke from off you \q and snap the ropes that bind you.

L.13: And now I will break his yoke from upon you, \q and I will tear apart your bonds.

R.13: Now I will break the yoke the Assyrians put on you. \q I will tear off the ropes that tie you up.

decisions.choice: his yoke ... your bonds: Assyria's rule over Judah
decisions.reason: A yoke is the wooden bar laid on the neck of an ox, held by ropes or straps. It is a common picture of foreign rule and the tribute it demanded (Isaiah 10:27; Jeremiah 27:2; 28:10-14). "His" is the Assyrian, the oppressor of verses 11 and 14.

decisions.choice: Judah under Assyria
decisions.reason: From the time of King Ahaz (about 734 BC) Judah was a subject state of Assyria and paid it heavy tribute (2 Kings 16:7-8; 18:14). Hezekiah's revolt led to Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC, and Manasseh remained a subject of Assyria.

decisions.choice: the ropes that bind you (B); the Assyrians (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "ropes" for the bonds that hold a yoke in place. Readable names the Assyrians as the "he" whose yoke it is (m1).

records.source: וְצִוָּ֤ה עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ יְהוָ֔ה לֹֽא־יִזָּרַ֥ע מִשִּׁמְךָ֖ ע֑וֹד מִבֵּ֨ית אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ אַכְרִ֨ית פֶּ֧סֶל וּמַסֵּכָ֛ה אָשִׂ֥ים קִבְרֶ֖ךָ כִּ֥י קַלּֽוֹתָ׃פ
records.gloss: And Yahweh has commanded concerning you: Not will be sown from your name again; from [the] house of your gods I will cut off carved image and cast image; I will make your grave, for you are of no account.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has given a command about you: \q you will have no more offspring to bear your name. \q I will cut off the carved idol and the cast image from the house of your gods. I will make your grave, for you count for nothing.

L.14: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has commanded concerning you: \q No more [offspring] of your name will be sown; \q from the house of your gods I will cut off carved image and cast image; I will make your grave, for you are of no account.

R.14: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has given an order about you, king of Assyria: \q You will have no children to carry on your name. \q I will destroy the idols and metal statues in the temple of your gods. I will dig your grave, because you are worthless.

decisions.choice: you: the king of Assyria
alternatives: the people of Nineveh as a whole
decisions.reason: "You" is now masculine singular. It is most likely the king of Assyria, who is addressed by name in 3:18, though it could be Nineveh's people taken as one.

decisions.choice: no more will be sown from your name: you will have no descendants
decisions.reason: Seed is the Hebrew word for offspring. To have no more "sown" of one's name is to have no descendants to keep it alive (compare Isaiah 14:22). The king's line, and with it the empire, will end.

decisions.choice: carved image and cast image in the house of your gods
decisions.reason: A carved image was cut from wood or stone; a cast image was made of molten metal (Deuteronomy 27:15). The house of the gods is a temple. Sennacherib was killed by his own sons while he worshiped in the temple of his god (2 Kings 19:37), and the gods of Nineveh could not save it.

decisions.choice: I will make your grave, for you are of no account
alternatives: I will make the house of your gods your grave
decisions.reason: "Of no account" is literally "light", without weight or honor, the opposite of "heavy", which is the word for glory. The first clause may also be read "I will make it (the house of your gods) your grave".

decisions.choice: no more offspring to bear your name (B); no children to carry on your name (R); worthless (B, R); king of Assyria (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the picture of sowing (m2). Readable names the king of Assyria as the one addressed (m1), and marks it as likely rather than certain.
